sections.title: From a neuron to agents that communicate
teaching: A **single neuron** multiplies its inputs by weights and adds the products into one number. A **neural network** combines these operations into layers, turning one input vector into a decision vector.

An **LLM** processes fifteen vectors through successive layers and predicts a sixteenth vector, a probability distribution over the next token. An **agentic system** joins whole LLMs into a graph that outlines, writes, criticizes, revises and finalizes the response.
The critic and reviser form a loop so a revised draft can be evaluated again. The agents communicate in English and can work in other human languages and computer languages.
**Inference uses inner products**, while learning uses **SGD and dynamic programming**. Inference processes current inputs with learned weights, while learning changes the weights to reduce error.

Click 1: one neuron — a vector comes in, one number comes out (an inner product).
Click 2: a small network, layers 4-3-4-5 — each W turns a vector into a vector; the last layer is a decision vector.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers
teaching: **Predicting the next word is difficult**, so an LLM uses many layers to develop its input representations. Each layer transforms the vectors produced by the preceding layer.

Within a layer, **heads work in parallel as different experts**. Their contributions are combined into new representations, and the next layer repeats the process with those representations. Heads contribute within one stage, while layers provide successive stages.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth
teaching: A **dynamical system** applies a rule to its state and feeds the resulting state back in. In the oscillator, position is updated using the old velocity, then velocity is updated using that new position. Repeating the rule produces oscillation.

In **Jordan’s recurrent network**, plan and state units feed a hidden layer, output returns to state units, and self-connections preserve a fading trace. The weights are reused over time, so recent outputs affect the next output.

An **LLM** transforms vectors through successive layers, so depth plays the role of time. Following one number through the layers gives a changing curve. Each layer has its own weights, unlike the same rule reused across time in the oscillator and recurrent network.
The small stock-return graph traces Small, Medium and Large series fluctuating over the same period, another example of quantities changing over time.

sections.speakerNotes:
Click 1: the machine. Numbers go in, a rule acts, numbers come out, and the output is fed back in as the next input. The numbers shown are the oscillator's first step (x0 = 1, v0 = 0, h = 2π/16).
Click 2: the harmonic oscillator, played automatically. x and v take turns: x(n+1) uses v(n); then v(n+1) uses the new x(n+1). The orange arrows show this interleaving for the first two steps. The dots trace a cosine (x) and a minus-sine (v). (This interleaved update is the symplectic Euler rule, which is why the curve does not spiral out.)
Click 3: Jordan's 1986 network. Plan and state units feed the hidden layer, which feeds the output; the output is copied back into the state units, which also keep a decaying copy of themselves (the small loops). Same W's every step.
Click 4: an LLM drawn as layers only, with the 15 vectors between them.
Click 5, played automatically: the rule is applied layer by layer (W1 ... W5). Follow one number in each vector up through the stack and you get a curve, built point by point as in the oscillator, but not sinusoidal. Depth is the LLM's time. One difference to point out: in the oscillator and the Jordan net the same rule is reused every step; in an LLM each layer has its own W.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences
teaching: An **LLM** receives fifteen vectors and predicts the following one. The vectors can represent words in a sentence, frames of a spectrogram, patches of a picture, or amino acids in the **insulin B chain**.

The picture is divided into sixteen patches, with fifteen given and the bottom-right patch left to predict. In the protein example the next residue is Y. The original materials differ, but all are represented as **sequences of vectors**.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?
teaching: One-syllable words like Don, mat and fish follow a **consonant, vowel, consonant** pattern. Clusters are allowed **before and after the vowel** only in certain orders, so split, flat, desk and help are words while *sblit, *lfat, *desb and *hepl are impossible, with the order mirroring around the vowel.

A **long word is a chain of syllables**, each obeying the same rules. t·l is fine across a break in At·lan·tic, but **tl cannot start a syllable**, so *tlantic is impossible, and ng can end a syllable but never start one.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge
teaching: Guessing the **next letter** of a word start shows **phonotactic knowledge**. After a vowel, as in **ra_**, almost anything can follow. At the start of a word the choices narrow, to **l, r or a vowel** after sp_, b_ and f_, and to **only a vowel** after skr_ and m_.

Each item also has an impossible continuation, such as *spn, *kt, *skrl or *mb. **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆**, so a **GPT** trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, with a broad distribution after ra_ and a sharply peaked one after skr_.

sections.title: What an LLM learns
teaching: An LLM learns by guessing a **hidden word**. In “The chef cracks the,” each earlier word gives a clue about the last word, and these links are **interdependencies**. The model spreads its bets over “egg,” “nut” and “code,” with the largest bet on “egg.”
**Learning is nudging the weights** so the right word gets a bigger bet next time. The same idea holds when the signal contains words, sounds and images.

sections.title: Text, speech and images in three different forms
teaching: Text is **already a row of pieces**, so each piece can become a vector. Speech is **air pressure changing in time**, and an image is **a grid of light**. Neither one contains words.
An LLM can only read a row of vectors. Speech and images therefore have to be **converted into rows of vectors** before the model can read them with text.

questions.prompt: Explain how an LLM learns from the sentence “The chef cracks the ?”.
questions.answer: The LLM learns by guessing the hidden last word and then changing its weights. Each earlier word gives a clue about the hidden word, so the model bets most on “egg” and less on “nut” and “code.” When the true word is revealed, the weights are nudged so the right word gets a bigger bet next time.
rubric: State that the model guesses the hidden word from the earlier words.
State that the weights are nudged so the right word gets a bigger bet.

questions.prompt: Why does the model bet on “egg,” “nut” and “code” instead of giving one answer?
questions.answer: The model spreads its bets because it does not know the hidden word. All three words could follow “The chef cracks the.” The earlier words make “egg” the most likely, so “egg” gets the largest bet, “nut” gets a smaller one and “code” gets the smallest.
rubric: Explain that the model does not know the answer.
Explain that the earlier words make some words more likely than others.

questions.prompt: Compare the forms in which text, speech and an image arrive before conversion.
questions.answer: Text is already a row of pieces, such as “Now,” “crack,” “the” and “egg.” Speech is air pressure changing in time, and an image is a grid of light. Speech and images contain no words, so they are not yet in a form the LLM can read.
rubric: Describe text as a row of pieces.
Describe speech as air pressure in time and an image as a grid of light.

questions.prompt: Why do speech and images have to be converted before an LLM can use them?
questions.answer: Speech and images have to be converted because a row of vectors is all the LLM can read. Speech is air pressure changing in time, and an image is a grid of light, so neither one is a row of vectors. Once they are converted, the model can read them in one row together with text.
rubric: State that the LLM reads only rows of vectors.
State that speech and images do not arrive as rows of vectors.

questions.prompt: Describe how speech is turned into a row of vectors.
questions.answer: Speech is turned into vectors by slicing it in time. First the sound is cut into short slices called frames, each about 20 milliseconds long. Then the slices go through a speech encoder, which is a network trained on a large amount of audio. One vector comes out for each slice, and the vectors stay in time order.
rubric: Describe slicing into frames of about 20 milliseconds.
Describe the speech encoder giving one vector per slice in time order.

questions.prompt: Why does one second of speech become 50 vectors?
questions.answer: One second of speech becomes 50 vectors because each slice gets one vector. Each slice is about 20 milliseconds long, and 50 slices of that length fill one second. The speech encoder gives one vector per slice, so one second gives 50 vectors.
rubric: Link the count to slices of about 20 milliseconds.
State that each slice gives one vector.

questions.prompt: Describe how an image is turned into a row of vectors.
questions.answer: An image is turned into vectors by cutting it into patches. First a grid cuts the image into small squares called patches, 16 of them in the egg example. Then the patches are laid out in a row in reading order, so the image becomes a sequence. A vision encoder then gives one vector for each patch.
rubric: Describe cutting into patches and laying them out in reading order.
Describe the vision encoder giving one vector per patch.

questions.prompt: Give one similarity and one difference between converting speech and converting an image.
questions.answer: The similarity is that both are cut into small pieces, and an encoder gives one vector for each piece, in order. The difference is what is cut. Speech is cut in time into frames of about 20 milliseconds. An image is cut in space into square patches, which are then placed in reading order.
rubric: Give the shared steps of cutting into pieces and encoding one vector per piece.
Contrast cutting in time into frames with cutting in space into patches.

questions.prompt: What is a cross-modal dependency? Give an example from “Now crack the ?”.
questions.answer: A cross-modal dependency is a link in which a piece from one sense helps predict a piece from another sense. In “Now crack the ?”, an image patch containing an egg helps predict the hidden word. The sound of cracking helps too. These clues come from the image and the sound, not from the earlier words.
rubric: Define the link as running between different senses.
Give the egg patch or the cracking sound as a clue for the hidden word.

questions.prompt: When the row holds three senses, what is the same as with text alone, and what is different?
questions.answer: The game is the same. The model still guesses the hidden piece from the pieces it can read, and the earlier words still give clues. The difference is where the clues come from. With three senses in the row, some clues come from image patches and speech frames.
rubric: State that the guessing game and the word clues stay the same.
State that some clues now come from other senses.

questions.prompt: Explain how to read the spectrogram of “three cute puppies.”
questions.answer: In the spectrogram, time runs from left to right, so “three” comes first and “puppies” comes last. A higher position means a higher frequency. A darker area means more energy. Each thin column is one frame.
rubric: Give time as left to right and frequency as height.
Give darkness as energy.

questions.prompt: What does “three views of one event” mean for “three cute puppies”?
questions.answer: The image, the spoken phrase and the written words all describe the same thing, which is three cute puppies. The image gives it as patches, the speech gives it as frames, and the text gives it as words. In training, all three go into one row, and the model guesses a hidden piece of that row.
rubric: Identify the three forms as the image, the speech and the words.
State that training puts all three into one row.

questions.prompt: Compare the model’s bets with text alone and with the image and sound added.
questions.answer: With text alone, the bets are spread out over “kittens,” “puppies” and “babies,” because many endings fit “three cute.” With the image and the sound, the bet piles up on “puppies.” This is because the image contains puppies and the sound contains the spoken word “puppies.”
rubric: Describe spread-out bets with text alone.
Explain that the image and the sound move the bet onto “puppies.”

questions.prompt: The model bet 0.85 on “puppies.” Why is the nudge to the weights small?
questions.answer: The nudge is small because the error is small. The model is graded on how much it bet on the true word. It bet 0.85 on “puppies,” which is a lot, so there is little to correct and the weights move only a little.
rubric: Link the high bet on the truth to a small error.
Link the small error to a small change in the weights.

questions.prompt: What would happen to the nudge if the model had bet only a little on “puppies”?
questions.answer: The nudge would be larger. A small bet on the true word means a large error. A larger error moves the weights more, so that next time the true word gets a bigger bet.
rubric: State that the error would be larger.
State that the weights would move more.

questions.prompt: Name the three clues the model uses to predict a hidden sound frame, and say what each one gives.
questions.answer: The earlier frames help because the voice and the formants change smoothly, so the last few frames say a lot about the next one. The words say which sound should come next, which here is the vowel in “pup.” The image contains puppies, so it backs up the words, but it is a weaker clue here.
rubric: Explain the earlier frames through smooth change in voice and formants.
Explain what the words and the image add.

questions.prompt: What is the error when the model guesses a sound frame?
questions.answer: A frame is a column of numbers, and each number is how much energy there is in one frequency band. The model’s guess is another column of numbers. The error is how far apart each number in the guess is from the matching number in the true frame. That error nudges the weights.
rubric: Describe a frame as energy values across frequency bands.
Describe the error as the difference between guess and truth, number by number.

questions.prompt: Explain what each clue gives the model when it predicts the hidden image patch.
questions.answer: The earlier patches give background above and two puppies to the left, so the model has seen what a puppy in this image looks like. The word “three” says a third puppy must appear, and “puppies” says to expect dog ears. The sound carries the same words, so it backs up the text.
rubric: Explain what the earlier patches give.
Explain what “three” and “puppies” give, with the sound as a backup.

questions.prompt: Why is the colour the biggest error when the model guesses the hidden patch?
questions.answer: The colour is the biggest error because no clue gave the colour of the third puppy. The model guessed a puppy ear in the average colour of the first two puppies. The true puppy is dark, and nothing in the words, the sound or the earlier patches said so.
rubric: State that no clue gave the third puppy’s colour.
State that the guess used the average colour of the first two puppies.

questions.prompt: Which systems are trained to predict image patches, and which usually are not?
questions.answer: Only systems that also produce images are trained to predict image patches. Systems that only read images usually skip this step. Predicting a patch is like teaching the model to draw what it was told, so it matters only when the system has to draw.
rubric: Identify systems that produce images.
State that systems that only read images usually skip this step.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a clue from the same sense and a clue from another sense?
questions.answer: A clue from the same sense mostly says how the signal continues. Grammar does this for a hidden word, smooth formants do it for a hidden frame, and fur and background do it for a hidden patch. Clues from the other senses mostly say what the thing is, which here is puppies, three of them.
rubric: State that same-sense clues say how the signal continues.
State that other-sense clues say what the thing is.

questions.prompt: Why does training on words, sound and images together help?
questions.answer: Training on all three senses together helps because each sense fills gaps the others leave. A clue from the same sense says how the signal continues. Clues from the other senses say what the thing is. With all three, the model has both kinds of clue for every hidden piece.
rubric: State that each sense fills gaps the others leave.
Refer to the two kinds of clue.

questions.prompt: Explain how the model talks back.
questions.answer: The model talks back by predicting sound codes. First, sound is compressed into discrete codes, and each code works like a new word in the vocabulary. Then the model predicts the next code exactly as it predicts the next word. Last, a decoder turns the codes back into a sound wave.
rubric: Describe sound compressed into codes that act like new words.
Describe predicting the next code and decoding back into sound.

questions.prompt: What three things are new when an LLM is trained on words, sounds and images?
questions.answer: The first new thing is a shared currency, in which everything becomes vectors in one row. The second is data where the senses appear together. The third is a schedule that protects what was already learned.
rubric: Give the shared currency of vectors in one row.
Give data with the senses together and the protective schedule.

questions.prompt: What stays the same when the signal holds words, sounds and images?
questions.answer: The learning rule stays the same. The model still finds the dependencies in the signal by guessing a hidden piece and nudging its weights. The signal has become wider, because it now holds words, sounds and images.
rubric: State that the model still finds dependencies in the signal.
State that only the content of the signal has widened.
